goal.outcome: Decide within 12 months whether to buy a main-street business (HVAC, services, light manufacturing) via SBA 7(a) financing, with a concrete financing structure and diligence checklist ready to execute.
constraints: Main-street business size (roughly under $5M purchase price)
success: A target deal identified and put under LOI
Financing structure (equity/seller note/SBA split) confirmed with a lender
Full diligence completed without a disqualifying finding
Clear go/no-go decision made before month 12, even if the decision is 'not yet'

approach.recommended: Follow the standard SBA 7(a) acquisition structure: 10% equity injection (up to half of it seller-note-eligible on standby), 80-85% SBA-guaranteed loan, targeting a business priced 2.0-3.5x SDE (or 4-6x EBITDA if over $1M earnings) that clears 1.25x DSCR.
approach.why: This is the best-documented, most consistent path across sources (S1-S4), with concrete guardrails (DSCR check, working capital peg, add-back scrutiny) that protect a first-time buyer from the most common failure modes.

alternatives.why_not: Single-source, thin on specifics, requires a narrow type of highly motivated seller, and gives up structural protections the mainstream path relies on.

alternatives.option: Skip QoE, use bookkeeper review for sub-$2M deals
alternatives.why_not: Saves ~$15k but trades away the rigor that catches inflated add-backs — a real risk-for-cost tradeoff, not a free lunch; acceptable only as a fallback on very small deals.

first_steps.action: Total your liquid capital and run it against the deal calculator structure.
first_steps.detail: Use a spreadsheet like C9 (purchase price, 10% down, up to 5% seller note, 80-85% SBA, rate ~prime+2.5-3%) to see what purchase price range your actual cash supports before searching.

first_steps.action: Call 2-3 SBA 7(a) lenders and ask about your borrower profile.
first_steps.detail: Ask specifically: do you need industry experience or a named manager in place? What's their current rate and closing timeline? Rates/timelines can vary by a full point and a month between lenders.

first_steps.action: List your industry-experience gap honestly and decide how to close it.
first_steps.detail: If you lack HVAC/services/manufacturing operating experience, decide now whether to target a business with a strong #2/GM staying on, or to build relevant experience first.

first_steps.action: Pick your target sub-sector and pull 3-5 comparable recent sale listings.
first_steps.detail: Check BizBuySell or a broker for asking multiples in your chosen niche to sanity-check the 2-3.5x SDE range vs. the contested 4-6x HVAC/plumbing claim.

phases.name: 1. Readiness & lender pre-check
phases.objective: Confirm you can actually finance a deal before spending time sourcing one.

tasks.detail: Determine max purchase price your liquid cash + eligible seller-note stacking supports at 10% equity injection.
Get informal feedback on your profile, experience gap, and likely rate/terms.

tasks.task: Decide target sector and price band
tasks.detail: Choose between HVAC/services (higher multiple risk) vs. light manufacturing (steadier multiples) based on comps.

phases.outcome: A defined price range and lender relationship(s) before you start looking at businesses.

phases.name: 2. Sourcing
phases.objective: Build a pipeline of realistic targets.

tasks.detail: Baseline source, but expect picked-over/overpriced deals.
Anecdotally the best deals come from direct contact, not brokers — worth testing even though single-sourced.

phases.outcome: A shortlist of 3-5 candidate businesses to evaluate.

phases.name: 3. Offer & LOI
phases.objective: Get a signed LOI on the best candidate with the right protective terms.

tasks.task: Price the offer explicitly on stated SDE
tasks.detail: State the exact SDE figure the offer is based on to avoid disputes later.
Reference the peg concept in the LOI even before the exact number is set.
These are the only truly binding LOI terms; everything else can be renegotiated.
Long enough to diligence, short enough to stop the seller shopping the deal.

phases.outcome: Signed LOI on one target, exclusivity secured.

phases.name: 4. Diligence (the 90-day window)
phases.objective: Validate the deal or kill it before closing.

tasks.task: Commission a QoE report (or bookkeeper review for <$2M deals)
tasks.detail: $8k-$20k, ties tax returns to bank statements; validates SDE.
Only count add-backs that genuinely disappear once seller leaves.
Any single customer >20% of revenue is a hard flag/deal-killer.
Non-assignable leases kill more deals than bad financials — check early.

tasks.task: Finalize the working capital peg number
tasks.detail: Lock the exact receivables+inventory-payables figure the seller must deliver.

tasks.task: Run the DSCR check with your actual lender
tasks.detail: Confirm 1.25x DSCR at the agreed price and structure before proceeding to close.

decisions: Go / no-go on this specific deal
phases.outcome: A financeable, verified deal ready to close, or a clean walk-away.

phases.name: 5. Close & first 90 days
phases.objective: Close the loan and stabilize the business without losing revenue.

tasks.detail: Prepare the core application package the lender requires ahead of time to avoid delay.

tasks.task: Structure seller transition with a holdback
tasks.detail: Keep seller involved ~90 days post-close, secured via holdback in the purchase agreement.
No firing/major changes except active safety issues; priority is retaining existing revenue, not optimizing.

phases.outcome: Business acquired and stabilized, revenue retained through transition.

dependencies.item: Confirmed liquid capital for 10% equity injection
dependencies.note: Determines max deal size; must be known before serious sourcing.
Could stall approval later if not addressed early.

dependencies.item: Working capital peg agreed in LOI
dependencies.note: Needed before close, not before LOI, but should be referenced early.

decisions.decision: Target sector: HVAC/plumbing vs. other services/light manufacturing
decisions.recommended: Lean toward less roll-up-affected sub-sector unless local comps confirm HVAC multiples are still reasonable
decisions.why: PE roll-ups may be pushing HVAC/plumbing multiples to 4-6x per one contrarian claim; unverified but worth hedging against.

decisions.decision: Full QoE report vs. bookkeeper review
decisions.recommended: Full QoE unless deal is under $2M and cash-constrained
decisions.why: QoE is the single most important diligence document; the cheaper substitute trades away rigor on the exact issue (inflated add-backs) most likely to bite.

decisions.decision: How much seller note to use toward equity injection
options: Use less / rely on more cash
decisions.recommended: Use seller note up to the allowed 50% of injection if seller will accept full standby terms
decisions.why: Cuts real cash-to-close roughly in half; only constraint is many sellers refuse standby.

tools.free_option: Build your own (mirror C9 structure: price, down%, seller note%, SBA amount, DSCR)
tools.why: Lets you quickly test whether a target deal clears 1.25x DSCR before spending on diligence.

tools.free_option: Bookkeeper bank statement review (sub-$2M deals only)
tools.why: Validates seller's SDE claims against bank statements; catches inflated add-backs.
Primary and secondary channels for finding candidate businesses.

upfront.item: Equity injection (10% of purchase price, cash portion)
upfront.amount: e.g. $50k-$100k on a $1M deal, less if seller note stacked in
Scales with loan size; can be rolled into loan (est. low-to-mid thousands)

recurring.amount: Prime + 2.5-3%, amortized over up to 10 years (25 if real-estate-heavy)

optional.item: Bookkeeper review instead of full QoE (sub-$2M deals)
optional.amount: Saves ~$15,000 vs full QoE, at a rigor cost

services.amount: Varies by lender; compare rate/timeline across 2-3 lenders

costs.contingency: Budget an extra 10-15% of equity injection cash for closing costs, working capital shortfall, and post-close surprises.
costs.minimum: ~$50k-$100k liquid cash for a $1M-scale deal assuming max seller-note stacking
costs.recommended: $100k-$150k liquid cash to comfortably clear equity injection plus contingency on a $1M-$1.5M deal
costs.premium: $250k+ liquid cash gives flexibility for a $2M+ deal or a deal without seller-note stacking
costs.note: All figures scale with target purchase price; run your own numbers through the deal calculator structure before committing to a price band.

risks.risk: Personal guarantee exposure on the full SBA loan (unlimited, for any 20%+ owner)
risks.mitigation: Explicitly weigh this against personal risk tolerance before signing the LOI, independent of financing side debate.

risks.risk: Deal priced above what DSCR will support, wasting diligence spend
risks.mitigation: Run DSCR math (1.25x minimum) before committing to a QoE report or advancing past LOI.

risks.risk: Customer concentration >20% discovered late in diligence
risks.mitigation: Ask for revenue-by-customer breakdown early, before paying for a full QoE.

risks.risk: Non-assignable lease kills the deal after months of work
risks.mitigation: Check lease assignability in the first week of diligence, not the last.

risks.risk: Inflated add-backs overstate SDE and you overpay
risks.mitigation: Apply the strict add-back test and verify via QoE tie-out to bank statements.

risks.risk: Lender rejects you for lack of industry experience/management
risks.mitigation: Pre-check with lenders before spending time sourcing; line up a GM candidate if needed.

risks.risk: Post-close revenue loss from premature operational changes
risks.mitigation: Preserve status quo for 90 days except active safety issues; prioritize revenue retention.

gotchas.gotcha: First-time buyers forget the working capital peg and can end up buying an empty balance sheet if the seller strips receivables pre-close.
gotchas.avoid: Reference the peg concept in the LOI before the exact number is finalized, and lock it before closing.

gotchas.gotcha: SBA fees and guarantee costs seem like extra out-of-pocket cash but can usually be rolled into the loan.
gotchas.avoid: Ask the lender explicitly which fees are rollable before assuming your cash-to-close is higher than it is.

gotchas.gotcha: The 'multiple' quoted by sellers/brokers is often SDE-based even for larger deals where EBITDA is the right metric.
gotchas.avoid: Confirm whether you're above the ~$1M earnings threshold and switch to EBITDA-based comparison if so.

gotchas.gotcha: Seller notes only count toward equity injection if fully on standby — many sellers will resist this.
gotchas.avoid: Raise the standby requirement early in negotiations, not after the LOI is signed.

defer.until: After the first 90 days of status-quo stabilization

defer.item: Choosing between full QoE vs bookkeeper review
defer.until: Once a specific deal and its size are known (Phase 4)
Only relevant if a target deal includes significant real estate

open_questions.question: How much liquid capital do you actually have available for the equity injection?
open_questions.why: Determines the entire price range you can realistically pursue.
open_questions.research_prompt: List your liquid savings, investments, and any accessible retirement/rollover funds usable for a business acquisition equity injection.

open_questions.question: Do you have relevant industry experience, or is there a manager/GM who could stay on post-close?
open_questions.why: Lenders explicitly weigh this; it affects both loan approval odds and target deal selection.
open_questions.research_prompt: Contact 2 SBA lenders and ask what level of industry experience or management continuity they require for approval on a deal your size.

open_questions.question: Are HVAC/plumbing multiples in your specific target geography actually running 4-6x, or is that a national/anecdotal claim?
open_questions.why: Materially changes whether home services is an affordable target sector.
open_questions.research_prompt: Pull 3-5 recent comparable business sale listings/asking prices in your target metro area and sub-sector, and compare implied SDE multiples.

open_questions.question: What is your risk tolerance for the unlimited personal guarantee required on the SBA loan?
open_questions.why: This is irreversible personal exposure and should shape whether you pursue SBA at all vs. explore partial alternatives.
open_questions.research_prompt: N/A — this is a personal risk-tolerance decision, not a research question.

open_questions.question: Is real estate likely to be part of your target deal?
open_questions.why: Changes maturity terms (10 vs up to 25 years) and total project cost calculations.
open_questions.research_prompt: N/A — depends on which specific business you pursue.

Standard 2-3.5x SDE range is well-supported, but the HVAC/plumbing 4-6x claim is single-sourced and contrarian.
S3 gives a clear, internally consistent framework (QoE, add-backs, concentration, peg, assignability).
Only one thin anecdotal data point on broker vs. direct outreach; no real strategy established.
Core principles (status quo, holdback, revenue retention) are solid but the source material is mostly low-signal filler.

this_week.action: Call or email 2 SBA-preferred lenders and ask about equity injection rules, experience requirements, current rates, and typical closing timeline.

this_week.why: Lenders weigh this heavily; better to plan around it now than discover it mid-process.

refine_questions.question: How much liquid cash (savings, investments, accessible retirement funds) do you have available today for an equity injection?
refine_questions.why: This single number sets your entire realistic price range and shapes every downstream phase.

refine_questions.question: Do you have direct industry experience in HVAC, services, or light manufacturing, or access to a manager who could run day-to-day operations post-close?
refine_questions.why: Lenders explicitly factor this into approval; determines whether you need to pivot toward hiring a GM or self-operate.

refine_questions.question: Which sub-sector are you leaning toward: HVAC/plumbing, another home service, or light manufacturing?
refine_questions.why: Changes the valuation multiple range you should expect and where roll-up competition (PE buyers) is a real risk.

refine_questions.question: What is your comfort level with an unlimited personal guarantee on the full SBA loan amount?

refine_questions.question: Are you open to a deal that includes real estate (longer maturity, larger total project cost) or do you want to keep it lease-based?
refine_questions.why: Changes maturity terms (10 vs up to 25 years) and total capital required.

refine_questions.question: How many hours per week can you dedicate to sourcing and evaluating deals over the next 12 months?

analysis.situation: You want to decide within 12 months whether to buy a main-street business (HVAC, services, light manufacturing) using an SBA 7(a) loan, and you need to know the financing structure, down payment rules, valuation logic, diligence checklist, and first-90-day plan. The brief doesn't specify your current cash on hand, industry experience, or credit profile, so this read treats those as open unknowns rather than assumed strengths. The research base is strong on SBA mechanics and valuation/diligence frameworks (S1-S4), but thin on execution realities — sourcing, negotiation, and post-close operations are mostly covered by a low-signal, filler-heavy transcript (S6) plus one contrarian outlier (S5) that rejects the SBA path entirely. That gap matters because the 'how do I actually find and close a deal' layer is where most real-world variance lives, and it's the weakest part of the evidence you have.

strengths.point: You've defined a clear decision horizon (12 months) and a specific financing mechanism (SBA 7(a)), which is more structure than most first-time buyers start with.
strengths.so_what: This lets you build a real diligence/financing checklist now instead of drifting through broker listings; use the 12-month clock to force milestone checkpoints (search, LOI, diligence, close).

weaknesses.point: No stated industry experience, existing management team, or capital amount on hand.
weaknesses.so_what: Most SBA lenders want relevant industry experience or a management team ready to run the business post-close [F2]; if you lack both, this is a gap to close before you go deal-hunting, not after.

weaknesses.point: No confirmed cash reserve mentioned for the required equity injection.
weaknesses.so_what: A full change-of-ownership SBA loan requires a minimum 10% equity injection [F26]; on a $1M deal that's $100k cash-equivalent [F45], so you need to verify liquidity before assuming a deal size is in reach.

opportunities.point: Seller notes can legally cover up to half the required equity injection if placed on full standby.
opportunities.so_what: This can cut real cash-to-close roughly in half on a typical deal, making a $1M+ acquisition reachable with less liquid capital than the sticker price implies.

opportunities.point: SBA upfront guarantee fees can be rolled into the financed loan rather than paid in cash.
opportunities.so_what: Reduces cash-to-close beyond just the down payment question, freeing capital for working capital or contingencies.

opportunities.point: Direct outreach to owners over 55 reportedly outperforms broker listings for sourcing good deals.
opportunities.so_what: If broker-listed deals feel picked-over or overpriced, building a direct-mail/cold-outreach pipeline to older owners may surface better opportunities, though this is a single anecdotal source.

threats.point: Non-assignable leases are described as killing more deals than bad financials.
threats.so_what: Lease assignability must be checked early in diligence, not left until the end, or you risk losing a deal you've already spent months and diligence fees on.

threats.point: Customer concentration above 20% from a single client is treated as a hard deal-killer by multiple sources, including the contrarian one.
threats.so_what: Screen for concentration risk before spending on a QoE report; it's one of the few things both mainstream and contrarian sources agree kills deals.

threats.point: Every 20%+ owner must give an unlimited personal guarantee on the SBA loan.
threats.so_what: This is a real personal financial exposure that should be weighed against your risk tolerance before signing an LOI, not discovered at closing.

threats.point: PE-driven roll-ups may be pushing HVAC/plumbing multiples above the traditional 2-3x range, per one contrarian source.
threats.so_what: If targeting home services, budget for the possibility of paying 4-6x rather than 2-3x, or focus search on less roll-up-heavy trades.

readiness.note: No confirmed liquid capital stated; need to size target deal against actual available cash plus possible seller-note stacking [F26,F27,F45,F46].
Not established whether you have relevant operating experience or a manager lined up, which lenders explicitly weigh [F2].
Research base (S1, S4, C1, C4) gives solid, consistent detail on SBA structure, rates, guarantees, and maturities.

Good grounding in SDE/EBITDA multiples and what moves them (S2), but real-world multiple has a live disagreement (2-3.5x standard vs. 4-6x contrarian claim for home services) that needs local market-checking [F30,F34].
S3 gives a clear, usable checklist: QoE, add-backs, concentration, working capital peg, assignability [F39,F40,F41,F32,F43].
Only one thin anecdotal data point (direct outreach vs. brokers) [F14]; no real sourcing strategy established yet.
Some solid points (90-day seller involvement with holdback, no-firing rule except safety, retain-revenue priority) but much of the source material here (S6) is low-signal filler [F44,F37,F38].

options.path: Standard SBA 7(a) acquisition (10% equity + up to 5% seller note counted toward it + 80-85% SBA loan)
options.summary: Follow the documented SBA structure: bring 10% of total project cost as equity (partially seller-note-eligible on standby), get an 80%+ SBA-guaranteed loan, target a business priced at 2-3.5x SDE (or 4-6x EBITDA if over $1M earnings) that clears 1.25x DSCR.
options.cost: ~10% of purchase price in cash/equity-equivalent, plus $8k-$20k for a QoE report and financing/closing fees (partially rollable into the loan)
options.time_to_result: Several months to find and diligence a target, then ~60-90 days from signed LOI to close per typical timelines [F3,F16]
options.why_fit: This is the mainstream, best-documented path in the research, with clear checklists and guardrails (DSCR check, working capital peg, personal guarantee awareness) that reduce blind spots for a first-time buyer.

options.path: 100% seller financing, no SBA, no down payment (contrarian approach)
options.summary: Pay full asking price over 5-7 years from business cash flow, avoiding SBA paperwork and personal guarantee, per the contrarian source.
options.cost: Little to no cash at close, but likely a higher effective price (full asking price, no negotiated multiple discount) and dependent entirely on convincing a seller to defer all payment.
options.time_to_result: Potentially faster close (no SBA underwriting delay) but requires finding a seller willing to take 100% deferred payment, which is a narrow subset of sellers
options.why_fit: This is a single-source, opinion-heavy, thinly-evidenced strategy that avoids the two things (financing rules, diligence rigor) the rest of the research treats as essential; workable only for a narrow type of motivated seller and a buyer comfortable with less structural protection.

options.path: Lower-cost, self-directed diligence on a sub-$2M deal (skip full QoE, use bookkeeper review)
options.summary: For a smaller deal, save the $8k-$20k QoE cost by having a bookkeeper review bank statements instead, per one practitioner's cost-saving substitution.
options.cost: Diligence cost drops from ~$8k-$20k to a fraction of that; still need the 10% equity injection and standard SBA mechanics
options.time_to_result: Similar 60-90 day closing window, possibly faster diligence phase
options.why_fit: Reasonable cost-saving tweak for smaller deals, but it trades away the rigor that catches inflated add-backs and earnings quality issues, which the primary diligence source treats as the most important document in the whole process [F39,F40] — a real tradeoff, not a free lunch.

assumptions.assumption: You have or can raise roughly 10% of a target deal's total project cost in liquid cash or standby seller-note-eligible capital.
assumptions.if_wrong: You'll be priced out of deals in your target range, or forced into much smaller acquisitions than planned.
assumptions.how_to_check: Run your actual liquid net worth against the deal calculator structure (down payment + seller note + SBA loan) [C9] for a few realistic price points before searching.

assumptions.assumption: The target business will clear a 1.25x DSCR at the multiple you're willing to pay.
assumptions.if_wrong: The lender will reject financing regardless of how good the deal looks on paper, wasting diligence spend.
assumptions.how_to_check: Before making an LOI, plug the seller's SDE, proposed structure, and rate into a DSCR calculation like the one in C9/F33 before committing further.

assumptions.assumption: You'll be able to satisfy lenders' preference for industry experience or a ready management team.
assumptions.if_wrong: Loan approval could stall or require a co-signer/manager hire before underwriting proceeds.
assumptions.how_to_check: Talk to an SBA lender early (before searching) to pressure-test your profile against F2's stated preference.

assumptions.assumption: Multiples in your target sector will fall in the standard 2-3.5x SDE range, not the 4-6x claimed for PE-driven HVAC/plumbing roll-ups.
assumptions.if_wrong: You may be structurally priced out of home services and should pivot to light manufacturing or a less roll-up-affected trade.
assumptions.how_to_check: Pull 3-5 comparable recent listings/sales in your specific sub-sector and geography before committing to a niche; treat F34's claim as unverified and single-sourced.

failure_patterns.pattern: Buying without a working capital peg, leaving the business with an effectively empty balance sheet after seller strips receivables pre-close.
failure_patterns.avoid: Negotiate and document a working capital peg in the LOI/purchase agreement before closing, even before the exact number is finalized.

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting inflated seller add-backs (salary, truck, cell phone) without verifying they genuinely disappear post-transition.
failure_patterns.avoid: Apply the strict test: a legitimate add-back must be an expense that truly goes away once the seller leaves, and get it tied to bank statements via a QoE report.

failure_patterns.pattern: Ignoring lease assignability until late in the process.
failure_patterns.avoid: Check lease assignability as an early, top-tier diligence item, not an afterthought.

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating personal guarantee exposure and treating SBA financing as risk-free just because it's the 'standard' path.
failure_patterns.seen_in: SBA lending summary + contrarian source (in disagreement, but both flag the same risk)
failure_patterns.avoid: Explicitly weigh the unlimited personal guarantee against your risk tolerance before signing an LOI, regardless of which side of the SBA-vs-no-SBA debate you land on.

failure_patterns.pattern: Making changes (firing staff, altering operations) too soon after close instead of preserving status quo.
failure_patterns.avoid: Prioritize revenue retention over optimization in the first 90 days; only override this for active safety issues.

analysis.verdict: The mainstream SBA 7(a) path (S1/S4) is well-documented and gives you a workable checklist for financing, valuation, and diligence — proceed on that basis, but only after you close two concrete gaps: your actual liquid capital for the 10% equity injection, and your standing with an SBA lender given the industry-experience preference. The contrarian no-money-down approach (S5) is under-evidenced and shouldn't replace SBA financing as your primary plan, though its concentration-risk point is worth heeding regardless. Treat the sourcing and first-90-days phases as the weakest-evidenced parts of your plan — the research here is mostly filler (S6) — and expect to supplement with direct lender conversations and your own outreach testing before finalizing a 12-month timeline.
